content: The number of individuals living with HIV who are eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) provides critical insight into the scale of services and resources required to meet treatment needs comprehensively. ART eligibility criteria differ by country and are defined in national policies and treatment guidelines, which are informed by scientific evidence, public health standards, global recommendations, and other considerations. Over the past decade, global recommendations have evolved to expand ART eligibility progressively. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, ART should be initiated for the following groups of HIV-positive individuals: 1. Anyone aged five years or older with a CD4 count of ≤500 cells/mm³. 2. All children over five years of age, regardless of CD4 count, if they are in WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 or have active tuberculosis (TB). 3. All children under five years old, including infants. 4. All pregnant and breastfeeding women. 5. All serodiscordant couples (where one partner is HIV-positive and the other is not). 6. All individuals co-infected with TB. 7. All individuals co-infected with hepatitis B who have chronic liver disease. At the population level, estimating the number of people eligible for ART relies on epidemiological models similar to those used to estimate the total number of people living with HIV. These models calculate eligibility by combining the number of individuals already receiving treatment (based on previous or current criteria) with those newly eligible under current guidelines but not yet receiving treatment. Modeled estimates are preferred over program data because program data often fail to capture individuals who are eligible but have not been identified. As ART eligibility criteria have expanded over the years, the number of eligible individuals is approaching the total number of people living with HIV. This makes comparisons of treatment coverage over time and across countries more complex. Additionally, the number of HIV-positive pregnant women eligible for services to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) is equivalent to the number of pregnant women living with HIV. This figure, ideally disaggregated by location, forms the basis for assessing the adequacy of PMTCT intervention coverage. In most settings, modeling is required to estimate the number of women eligible for PMTCT. In countries with near-universal antenatal care (ANC) coverage and systematic HIV testing of ANC clients, program data may reflect the number of HIV-positive pregnant women. However, some countries estimate this number by multiplying HIV prevalence from ANC surveillance by the annual number of births. This approach is only valid if ANC surveillance is representative of the entire country or if adjustments are made for biases, such as urban-focused surveillance. Estimation models, such as the UNAIDS-supported Spectrum modeling tool, are used to produce consistent HIV-related estimates globally. These models incorporate demographic data (e.g., population size, fertility, mortality, and migration rates) and program data (e.g., the number of people receiving ART and PMTCT care) to estimate the number of people living with HIV and those eligible for ART. For children, additional assumptions, such as mother-to-child transmission rates and survival times for HIV-positive children, are applied to estimate prevalence. Stigma and discrimination remain significant barriers to effective HIV prevention, care, and treatment. These issues often target key populations at higher risk of HIV, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs, as well as all individuals living with HIV. Stigma, rooted in ignorance, fear, or false beliefs, leads to negative societal judgments, while discrimination involves actions that deny individuals their rights. Both phenomena discourage people from seeking testing, adopting preventive behaviors, and enrolling in care and treatment services. Addressing stigma and discrimination requires training healthcare providers, implementing supportive policies, and collecting data to assess the prevalence of these barriers. The delivery of HIV prevention, care, and treatment services depends on the strength of the underlying health system. WHO identifies six essential building blocks for functional health services: service delivery infrastructure, the health workforce, medical products and technology, financing, information, and leadership and governance. Deficiencies in any of these components can compromise the system's ability to deliver HIV services effectively. Monitoring service availability, readiness, quality, and linkages is crucial to ensuring adequate HIV service delivery. Facility assessments can identify gaps in equipment, supplies, and staffing, while quality management methods and client feedback mechanisms can guide improvements in service delivery. Laboratory capacity is particularly important for HIV programs, as it supports diagnosis, ART monitoring (e.g., viral load and CD4 count testing), and the detection of opportunistic infections. Proficiency testing and external quality assurance schemes are essential to maintaining high standards of laboratory practices.
